text.p: Oil which hit a new post-Gulf War record that took it above $25 per barrel on Tuesday again eclipsed other commodity markets where prices were little changed or lower.
In Chicago, the Commodities Research Bureau Index added 0.75 points to finish at 246.24.

LME copper ended Tuesday with muted gains after strength to attack overhead barriers evaporated. As prices approached the key $1,970 per tonne level on the first afternoon ring, selling came in, stalling the advance at $1,968, as profit-taking and producer selling overwhelmed buyers, dealers said. It was disappointing that the market could not even stay above the $1,950 level, ending only $11 higher at $1,945, they added.

Aluminium broke through several layers of resistance as influential short-covering hit the market, but eased off its afternoon high of $1,363. Last business on the kerb was at $1,356, a healthy $30 gain from Monday.
Lead recovered from its slide to seven-month lows of $735 on Monday, ending the kerb at $750, up $12. Resistance is pegged at $760/1.
Tin also finished the day stronger at $6,000, up from $5,975 on Monday, but off its high of $6,015.
Nickel ended unchanged at $7,120 after exploring within a range of $7,155 to $7,100.
Zinc gained $7 to $1,022, just on the cusp of resistance.

London November futures for the benchmark North Sea Brent blend crude broke above $25 a barrel for the first time since the 1990/1991 Gulf War. But they eased later. Brent has shot up by $7 a barrel since mid-June, driven by concern over tensions in the Middle East and persistently low stocks of heating fuel in pre-winter Western markets.

Prices on the New York Mercantile Exchange (NYMEX) took a breather Tuesday depite news of Mideast turmoil that fueled Monday's sharp gains, but most traders were loathe to say the rally was over. Crude oil for November delivery ended 20 cents lower at $25.42 a barrel, after failing to top the $25.72 new post-Gulf War high hit overnight on NYMEX's electronic trading system.

In London, white sugar futures backed off their earlier highs in solid volume on Tuesday as players took profits after the rally inspired by the raws market ran its course, traders said. Shortly after the New York open, fund buying pushed the spot March contract 19 points higher to hit 11.05 cents/lb and the sudden strength dragged London values along. At 1554 GMT December stood 50 cents firmer at $322.70 after touching a high of $325.00. March was up $1.20 at $319.50, $2.00 below its intraday high, and total market volume was 2,405 lots.

Late local and fund selling drove CBOT wheat futures to a lower close, Chicago traders said. Wheat was firm in early dealings on mounting talk that U.S. soft red winter wheat acreage for 1997 may be trimmed by the late harvest of the U.S. soybean crop. A fair portion of the soft red winter wheat acreage is planted after the soy crop has been combined. Wheat futures closed 1-3/4 to 7-3/4 cents per bushel lower, with December down 7-3/4 at $4.21-3/4.
